title: Glacier National Park Travel Guide

hero.alt: Glacier National Park alpine peaks, lakes, and Going-to-the-Sun Road
hero.headline: Glacier National Park Travel Guide
hero.subheadline: Plan Glacier around Going-to-the-Sun Road, Logan Pass, Lake McDonald, Many Glacier, Two Medicine, St. Mary, and the glacial and Indigenous history of Montana's northern Rockies.

overview: Glacier National Park protects a spectacular section of the northern Rocky Mountains where ancient sedimentary rocks were thrust eastward, glaciers carved deep valleys and cirques, and hundreds of lakes now fill basins below sharp ridges. Going-to-the-Sun Road crosses the park's mountainous core, but seasonal snow means the full route is open only part of the year.

A strong first visit uses several park districts rather than one scenic drive. Give Going-to-the-Sun Road and Logan Pass a full day, spend separate time around Lake McDonald or St. Mary, and add Many Glacier or Two Medicine for longer hikes and a quieter sense of the park. Indigenous cultural connections, wildlife, fire, snow, and rapidly changing mountain weather belong in every plan.

highlights.title: Going-to-the-Sun Road
highlights.description: Cross roughly 50 miles of mountain terrain on one of the National Park Service's landmark engineering and scenic roads.

highlights.title: Glacial lakes and valleys
highlights.description: See Lake McDonald, St. Mary Lake, Swiftcurrent Lake, and hundreds of smaller basins carved or shaped by ice.

highlights.title: High-country hiking
highlights.description: Use Logan Pass, Many Glacier, and Two Medicine for trails into alpine meadows, passes, waterfalls, and glacial basins.

highlights.title: Indigenous and international landscape
highlights.description: Recognize more than 10,000 years of Indigenous connection and Glacier's 1932 union with Waterton Lakes as the world's first International Peace Park.

thingsToDo.title: Drive Going-to-the-Sun Road when the full route is open
thingsToDo.description: Going-to-the-Sun Road is the only paved road that crosses Glacier National Park from east to west, running roughly 50 miles between the Lake McDonald and St. Mary sides. Built through extraordinary mountain terrain in the early 20th century, it climbs to Logan Pass before descending past glacial valleys, waterfalls, cliffs, and alpine slopes. Snow removal can take weeks each spring and the alpine section closes in winter, so never assume a summer-style crossing is possible outside the core season. Vehicle-access rules and reservation systems can also change. Check current NPS road status before setting out and use shuttles when they fit your itinerary.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Logan Pass and Hidden Lake country
thingsToDo.description: Logan Pass sits on the Continental Divide at 6,646 feet and is the high point of Going-to-the-Sun Road. Boardwalk and trail routes climb through subalpine meadows where wildflowers, mountain goats, bighorn sheep, marmots, and sudden storms can all shape a visit. Hidden Lake Overlook is a popular objective, while the Highline Trail begins nearby for much longer hiking. The open alpine terrain is fragile; staying on constructed paths protects plants with extremely short growing seasons. Parking fills early when the road is fully open, which makes shuttle access particularly valuable.

thingsToDo.title: Spend time on Lake McDonald
thingsToDo.description: Lake McDonald is Glacier's largest lake, stretching about 10 miles and reaching more than 460 feet deep. Glaciers carved and deepened its valley, while colorful pebbles along parts of the shore come from the park's ancient sedimentary rocks. The lake's west-side setting offers paddling, boat tours, shoreline walks, historic Lake McDonald Lodge, and access to nearby trails. The water remains cold even during warm weather, and wind can build quickly. Use the lake as a base for a western park day rather than racing through it on the way to Logan Pass.

thingsToDo.title: Hike and watch wildlife in Many Glacier
thingsToDo.description: Many Glacier is one of the park's most celebrated hiking districts, with trails leading toward Grinnell Glacier, Iceberg Lake, Cracker Lake, and high passes between steep peaks. Swiftcurrent and Josephine lakes add boat and shoreline options, while bears, moose, bighorn sheep, and other wildlife are frequently present in the wider valley. Trail access, construction, and seasonal services can change, so check current conditions before the long drive into the district. Carry bear spray where recommended, know how to use it, travel with wildlife awareness, and never let a famous trail objective override a temporary closure.

thingsToDo.title: See St. Mary Lake and the park's east-side geology
thingsToDo.description: St. Mary Lake stretches beneath some of Glacier's most recognizable peaks and forms the scenic eastern approach to Logan Pass. Pullouts along Going-to-the-Sun Road reveal Wild Goose Island, layered mountain walls, burn mosaics, and tributary valleys. The rocks here help tell the story of the Lewis Overthrust, a major fault system that moved very old sedimentary rocks over much younger layers during Rocky Mountain building. Strong winds are common on the east side, and weather can change much faster than lower-elevation forecasts suggest. Pair overlooks with a walk to waterfalls or a boat trip when conditions and seasonal operations allow.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Two Medicine
thingsToDo.description: Two Medicine lies in the park's southeastern corner and was a major early visitor destination before Going-to-the-Sun Road shifted travel patterns northward. Lakes, waterfalls, forest, and steep peaks support routes to destinations such as Running Eagle Falls, Scenic Point, and backcountry passes. The district also sits within a landscape of profound Blackfeet cultural significance. Use interpretation and respectful place-based learning rather than viewing the mountains only through recreational language. Road and facility operations are seasonal, and the district can be windy, so check current access before driving from the main east-side corridor.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the North Fork and Bowman Lake carefully
thingsToDo.description: The North Fork district offers a quieter and less developed Glacier experience reached partly by narrow, rough roads. Bowman Lake is the best-known destination, a long glacial lake framed by mountain ridges and forest. Its appeal comes partly from limited infrastructure, which also means visitors must arrive prepared and cannot expect the same services found at Lake McDonald or St. Mary. Road conditions, fire restrictions, campground availability, and vehicle limits can change. Drive slowly through gateway communities, respect private land, and do not treat the North Fork as an off-road playground.

thingsToDo.title: Connect Glacier with Waterton and the International Peace Park story
thingsToDo.description: Glacier National Park was established in 1910. In 1932, Glacier and Canada's Waterton Lakes National Park were joined symbolically as Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park, recognized as the world's first international peace park. The designation reflects a mountain ecosystem and human landscape that cross an international boundary rather than stopping at it. Visitors do not need to cross into Canada to appreciate that history, but those who do must plan for border rules and separate national-park systems. The larger landscape also overlaps longstanding Blackfeet, Salish, Kootenai, and other Indigenous homelands that predate both countries' park boundaries.

bestTimeToVisit.title: Snow controls Glacier's high-country season
bullets: Summer offers the broadest road and trail access, but Logan Pass and major trailheads are busy and vehicle-access rules may apply.
Late spring can be beautiful at lower elevations while Going-to-the-Sun Road remains closed across the alpine section.
Fall brings cooler weather, fewer visitors, wildlife activity, and rapidly diminishing services as snow returns.
Winter is a quiet snow-travel season with most high-country roads closed to vehicles and many visitor services unavailable.

travelTips: Check Going-to-the-Sun Road status and current vehicle-access requirements before every cross-park plan.
Carry bear spray where appropriate, know how to deploy it, and follow NPS food-storage and wildlife-distance rules.
Use shuttles when available for Logan Pass and popular trailheads where parking can fill very early.
Plan Many Glacier, Two Medicine, and the North Fork as separate districts rather than short detours from the main road.
Carry layers and rain protection even on warm days; mountain weather and east-side winds can change rapidly.

faq.q: How many days should I spend in Glacier National Park?
faq.a: Three to five days is a strong first-visit range. That gives time for Going-to-the-Sun Road, a major hiking district, Lake McDonald or St. Mary, and weather flexibility.
No. The alpine section closes for winter and requires extensive snow removal before reopening. Opening and closing dates vary, so current NPS road status is essential.

Logan Pass offers accessible high-country trails when the road is open, while Many Glacier has some of the park's most famous longer hikes. Choose according to road access, bear closures, snow, weather, and your ability.

faq.q: Are there still glaciers in Glacier National Park?
faq.a: Yes, but the park's glaciers have declined greatly since the end of the Little Ice Age. The broader landscape was also carved by much larger ancient glaciers, so glacial geology remains visible everywhere even where modern ice is absent.

faq.q: Why is Glacier culturally important beyond recreation?
faq.a: The region has been used by Indigenous peoples for more than 10,000 years and remains culturally significant to Blackfeet, Salish, Kootenai, and other communities. The park also forms the U.S. half of the 1932 Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Glacier National Park is a protected northern Rocky Mountain landscape, not a city. Its major visitor districts are separated by steep terrain, long roads, and a strongly seasonal alpine climate.

sections.heading: Geography & geology
paragraphs: Ancient sedimentary rocks were displaced eastward along the Lewis Overthrust and later carved by repeated glaciation into sharp ridges, U-shaped valleys, cirques, and deep lakes. Modern glaciers occupy only a fraction of the terrain once covered by ice.

sections.heading: Indigenous and park history
paragraphs: Indigenous peoples have used this mountain landscape for more than 10,000 years, and Blackfeet, Salish, Kootenai, and other communities maintain cultural ties today. Glacier became a national park in 1910 and joined Waterton Lakes in the International Peace Park in 1932.

sections.heading: Outdoor & seasonal highlights
paragraphs: Hiking, backpacking, paddling, scenic driving, cycling under current road rules, wildlife observation, boating, fishing, and snow travel all depend strongly on snowpack and seasonal access.

sections.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: Going-to-the-Sun Road is the primary cross-park route when open, but Many Glacier, Two Medicine, and the North Fork require separate approaches. Build itineraries by district and leave room for weather and wildlife delays.
